privacy.title: Privacy notice for inquiries
privacy.intro: This notice explains what happens to the details you send through the inquiry form on this site, which is run by the consulting firm that uses Selah.
privacy.collect: Your organisation's name and sector; your name, role and job title, email and phone, and how you prefer to be reached; the services you're interested in, why now, and your message. Optionally, its size and ownership type, three light questions for family businesses, and your answers to the six self-check questions. We don't accept files through the form.
privacy.why: Only to respond to your inquiry, check it for conflicts of interest, and decide whether and how the firm can help. We don't sell it. We send you news about events and publications only if you tick the separate box for it, and you can stop it at any time.
privacy.who: The firm's administrators, and the one consultant they assign to your inquiry. Other clients never see it.
privacy.technical: To stop abuse, we keep a keyed one-way hash of your network address and browser, never the address itself, and allow a few inquiries per hour from one address.
privacy.keep: If we start working together, your inquiry becomes part of your client record. Otherwise the contact details and message are erased 12 months after the inquiry is closed, or 30 days for spam. We keep only anonymous figures, such as sector and size, for statistics.
privacy.rights: You can ask to see, correct or delete your details by replying to the email you receive from the firm, or by contacting the firm directly. Requests are answered within 30 days, in line with the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: These terms apply to everyone with a Selah account on this site. Selah is run by the consulting firm that invited you, to follow up its recommendations with its clients. Where your organization has a signed engagement or contract with the firm, that agreement comes first, and these terms fill in how the site is used.

sections.title: Your account
sections.body: Accounts are by invitation only and belong to one person. Keep your password to yourself, use two-factor sign-in where your role requires it, and tell your administrator or the firm at once if you think someone else has used your account. Your administrator can switch your account off when you leave.

sections.title: What you may do
sections.body: Use Selah for the work you were invited to: reading what is shared with you, updating your actions, submitting evidence and taking part in reviews and meetings. Upload only files you are entitled to share, and nothing that contains malware or someone else's personal data without a reason to share it.

sections.title: What you may not do
sections.body: Don't try to reach data that wasn't shared with you, another client's data in particular, test the site's security without the firm's written permission, or use automated tools to read or load it. Every refused attempt is recorded.

sections.title: Who owns what
sections.body: Your organization keeps ownership of the files and information it puts in Selah. The firm's recommendations, reports and other deliverables are governed by your engagement with the firm. Selah does not use your files to train any AI model.

sections.title: What is recorded
sections.body: Sign-ins, files opened, changes and refused attempts are kept in an audit log that nobody can edit, for at least 12 months. Your administrator can see what your organization's people did; the firm's administrator can see everything.

sections.title: What the site does not do
sections.body: Selah tracks implementation. A status, a percentage or an AI answer is not a certification, an audit opinion or legal advice, and only a person at the firm verifies evidence. The site is provided as it is; the firm works to keep it available and safe but does not promise it will never be interrupted.

sections.title: Suspension and changes
sections.body: The firm may suspend an account that breaks these terms or puts others' data at risk. When these terms change, you will be asked to accept the new version at your next sign-in.

sections.title: Law
sections.body: These terms are governed by the laws of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

privacy.title: Privacy notice for account holders
privacy.intro: This notice explains what happens to your personal data when you use Selah with an account. The consulting firm that runs this site decides how it is used, in line with the Saudi Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL). The separate notice for the public inquiry form is at /privacy.

sections.title: What we hold
sections.body: Your name (and, if you give it, its spelling in the other language), your work email, your organization and role, your two-factor setting, the work you do in Selah (updates, evidence, comments, meetings) and the audit log of your sign-ins and actions, including the network address they came from.

sections.title: Why
sections.body: To run your organization's engagement with the firm, keep the site secure, show who did what, and meet the firm's legal duties. We don't sell your data or use it for advertising.

sections.title: Who sees it
sections.body: People on the same project see your name and your work on it. Your organization's administrator manages your account and sees your organization's activity. The firm's staff on your engagement see your work; the firm's administrator sees everything, including the audit log. Other clients never see anything about you.

sections.title: Where it is kept
sections.body: On the firm's own server in Saudi Arabia, with backups in a second location in the Kingdom. The services that may handle some of it in passing, such as delivering email, are listed at /legal/sub-processors.

sections.title: How long
sections.body: While your account is active, and then for as long as the engagement's records must be kept. The audit log is kept for at least 12 months. When your details are erased, your name and address are removed and only an anonymous id stays in the history, so the record of who did what still holds together.

sections.title: Your rights
sections.body: You can ask to see, correct or erase your personal data, or ask how it is used, through your organization's administrator or the firm directly. The firm answers within 30 days. You can also complain to the Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority (SDAIA).

sections.title: If something goes wrong
sections.body: If a breach puts your data at risk, the firm tells SDAIA within 72 hours where the law requires it, and tells you without undue delay what happened and what to do.

ai_notice.title: How Selah uses AI
ai_notice.intro: Selah has an assistant that helps the firm's consultants find and summarise what is already in the platform. This notice says what it reads, where it runs and what it never does.

sections.title: What it reads
sections.body: Only files whose AI setting is on and records the person asking is already allowed to open. Permissions are applied before anything reaches the model, so the assistant can't see what the person can't. Files are added to its index only when someone turns their AI setting on, and leave it when the setting goes off or the file is unshared or archived.

sections.title: Where it runs
sections.body: By default the model runs on the firm's own server, and nothing leaves it. If the firm switches to a hosted model, only the passages needed for one question are sent, with names of clients, people and departments masked first, and the provider is listed at /legal/sub-processors.

sections.title: What it never does
sections.body: It never approves evidence, closes an action, makes a governance or legal judgment, or certifies compliance. It never invents a recommendation. A person at the firm makes every decision, and everything the assistant writes is labelled as AI-written with its sources.

sections.title: Who can use it
sections.body: Today the firm's consultants and administrators. People at clients don't have the assistant, though summaries the firm shares with you may have been drafted with it and are labelled when so.

sections.title: What is kept
sections.body: The question and answer stay in the person's own chat, which is archived and then deleted on the firm's schedule. The audit log records that a question was asked and how many sources were used, never its text. Your files are never used to train a model.

sections.title: Your choice
sections.body: Ask the firm, or your administrator, to keep a file out of the assistant: its AI setting is switched off and it leaves the index at once.

data_agreement.title: Data processing agreement (template)
data_agreement.intro: A template for the agreement between the consulting firm and a client on the personal data the client puts in Selah. Clients sharing files fully or in restricted mode sign it before their files go in. The firm's lawyer adapts it; the blanks in [brackets] are filled for each client.

sections.title: 1. Parties and roles
sections.body: [Client name] (the Client) and [Firm name] (the Firm). For personal data in the files and records the Client puts in Selah, the Client decides why it is processed and the Firm processes it on the Client's behalf, only to carry out the engagement signed on [date].

sections.title: 2. What is processed
sections.body: Names, work contact details and roles of the Client's staff; personal data that appears in the documents the Client shares (such as policies, minutes and organisation charts); activity records in Selah. No special categories of data unless agreed in writing.

sections.title: 3. The Firm's duties
sections.body: Process only on the Client's documented instructions and for the engagement; keep the data confidential and limit access to the staff assigned to the Client; keep it in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia except where section 6 allows otherwise; apply the security measures in section 4; help the Client answer requests from data subjects within the 30 days the PDPL allows.

sections.title: 4. Security
sections.body: Separate access per client enforced in the database; two-factor sign-in for administrators and consultants; encryption in transit; virus scanning of every upload; an audit log that can't be edited, kept at least 12 months, with a nightly integrity check; encrypted nightly backups in a second location in the Kingdom, with a restore tested at least every quarter.

sections.title: 5. Breaches
sections.body: The Firm tells the Client within [24] hours of becoming aware of a breach affecting the Client's data, with what is known, the likely effects and what is being done, so the Client can notify SDAIA within 72 hours where required.

sections.title: 6. Sub-processors and transfers
sections.body: The Client accepts the services listed at /legal/sub-processors on the date of signing. The Firm gives [30] days' notice of a new one, and the Client may object. Data leaves the Kingdom only as the PDPL and its Transfer Regulation allow.

sections.title: 7. End of the engagement
sections.body: Within [30] days of the end, the Firm returns the Client's files as an export and deletes them from Selah and its backups, except what the law requires the Firm to keep, which stays protected for that period.

sections.title: 8. Audits and law
sections.body: The Client may ask for the Firm's security summary and, once a year with notice, check compliance with this agreement. This agreement is governed by the laws of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

security.title: Security overview for IT teams
security.intro: How Selah protects your organization's data, for your IT and security team to review. The panel below shows how this site is set up right now.

sections.title: Where it runs
sections.body: Selah runs on one server in Saudi Arabia that the firm operates. The database, the stored files, the virus scanner, the PDF renderer and, by default, the AI model all run on that server, each in its own container. Encrypted backups go nightly to a second location in the Kingdom.

sections.title: How traffic reaches it
sections.body: Every connection uses HTTPS. The site can be reached in one of two ways, shown under "This site, now": straight to the server, which holds its own certificates so nothing outside it sees the traffic; or through Cloudflare Tunnel, where Cloudflare ends HTTPS (it is listed as a sub-processor) and the server opens no port. The firm moves to the direct way before any real client file is uploaded. Browsers get strict security headers: HSTS, a content security policy with a fresh nonce per page, no framing.

sections.title: Keeping clients apart
sections.body: Each client's data is kept apart in the database itself: PostgreSQL row-level security decides, for every row, who may read it, keyed on the signed-in person. The application's database account cannot bypass it. Automated tests try to read across clients and roles on every change and must be refused.

sections.title: Accounts and sign-in
sections.body: Accounts are by invitation only, one per person, signed in with the person's own work email. Passwords are hashed with scrypt. Two-factor sign-in (an authenticator app) is required for the firm's administrators and consultants and for client administrators, and optional for others. Repeated failed sign-ins are slowed down and then locked. A client administrator can switch off their own people and runs periodic access reviews.

sections.title: Files
sections.body: Uploads are limited to 20 MB and to common document types, and every file is scanned for viruses before it is stored; the upload is refused while the scanner is down. Files sit in a private store under random names. A download is a link valid for one minute, issued only after the person's right to the file is checked.

sections.title: The AI assistant
sections.body: By default the model runs on the firm's server and nothing leaves it. If the firm switches to a hosted model, client, people and department names are replaced with placeholders before any text is sent, and only the passages needed for one question go. Files are never used to train a model. The firm can mark any file as not available to the assistant.

sections.title: Audit and monitoring
sections.body: Sign-ins, failed attempts, file views and downloads, changes and refused attempts are kept in an audit log that nobody can edit, sealed into a hash chain and checked every night, for at least 12 months. A client administrator sees what their own people did and can export it. The server checks its own health every two minutes and alerts the firm when something fails.

sections.title: Backups and recovery
sections.body: The database and the files are backed up every night, with an encrypted copy in a second location whose key is kept off the server. Backups are kept 30 days, so erased data leaves them within that time. A monthly drill restores a backup into a scratch database and checks it, row counts, audit chain and files included. At most a day of work can be lost.

sections.title: Incidents
sections.body: The firm follows a written breach runbook: contain, keep the evidence, assess, and notify. Under the data processing agreement a client is told within the agreed time (24 hours in the template) so it can notify SDAIA within 72 hours where required.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: Every change is reviewed and runs automated tests: unit tests, database rule tests including denial tests, and browser tests. Dependencies are watched for security updates. The controls are mapped to OWASP ASVS 5.0 and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications.

sections.title: Questions
sections.body: Your IT or security team can ask the firm's administrator for the detailed control list, the latest restore drill result, or a review session.
